extracted.intended_audience: copyright policymakers, administrative law scholars, and legal practitioners interested in small-claims/adjudicative reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for creating an administrative small-claims adjudicative forum (CIRP) within the Copyright Office, including procedural rules, structural features, remedies, and policy tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the small claims court within the federal court system
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping the small claims court within the federal court system could be a small step closer to providing a more efficient forum for small copyright owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserves the option to seek injunctive relief and could act as a “mini-trial” that would entice even wealthy plaintiffs to use the proceeding as a tryout for large cases. Downsides: does nothing to decrease burden on federal judiciary or delays; choosing whether to locate a federal small claims court in each district or only in a few districts near major IP centers is a logistical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a bench of dedicated judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a bench of dedicated judges would ensure the cases were handled by a court competent and familiar with the nuances of copyright law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing from senior judges for a specialized court can bring expertise to rulings (costs/benefits described by Greenspoon). Dedicated judges increase quality of decisions for IP-specific issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit non-attorneys to handle cases to lower costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If non-attorneys could successfully handle cases, as at the PCC, then some cost-savings would be realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing non-attorneys may reduce litigation costs and increase access, but the jurisdiction must ensure fairness and competency safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit discovery to reduce financial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Even minimally restricted discovery rules still place a hefty financial burden on small plaintiffs and defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CIRP design should minimize discovery (and related pre-litigation motions) to keep costs low and proceedings efficient; however overly restrictive discovery could impair fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic placement of fora: district-wide vs centralized IP centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to locate a federal small claims court in each federal district or just in a few districts close to major intellectual property centers (e.g., New York, Nashville, Los Angeles, and Washington, D.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization concentrates expertise but may reduce access; regional or circuit-rider ALJs and videoconferencing can mitigate access problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt TTAB features: written record and Accelerated Case Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The TTAB’s Accelerated Case Resolution (ACR) handles smaller, less complicated cases with fewer disputed facts by having parties stipulate that the TTAB can resolve disputed facts and rely on a written record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: avoids oral hearings, saves time and money; TTAB aims to make a decision within fifty days of considering the written record in ACR; caveat: TTAB often has similar or greater discovery burdens than district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge TTAB limitation: inability to grant injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The TTAB’s remedy is limited to determining registration/cancellation; if a trademark owner seeks damages or injunctions, he must go to federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A similar limitation for CIRP would reduce its ability to remove infringing material from the market; tradeoff between speed/low-cost relief and scope of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use VA-style nonadversarial, informal hearings to improve access
rubrics_metrics.description: The VA has a 'nonadversarial, informal system' for determining benefits; hearings are held in unimposing rooms, ALJ sits at same level as claimant, and formal rules of evidence do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting VA-style procedures could make hearings approachable for creators less adept at legal process, encourage pro se participation, and foster cooperation between administrators and claimants; critics note even pro-claimant systems need strong advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use SSA-style accessibility features: local hearings, ALJ duty to develop record, compulsion powers
rubrics_metrics.description: SSA hearings are held within seventy-five miles of a claimant’s home, ALJs have a positive duty to develop the record for unrepresented claimants, and ALJs can compel production of documents and witness appearances under oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying SSA features to CIRP could include voluntary local hearings, videoconferencing, and circuit-rider ALJs to increase convenience and ensure full development of the record—but would require investment or interagency partnerships for facilities and technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute CIRP as a panel of three ALJs modeled on CRJs
rubrics_metrics.description: The CIRP would be composed of a panel of three ALJs based in the Copyright Office, similarly qualified and recruited as the Copyright Royalty Judges (CRJs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing administrative staff supporting CRJs could provide needed infrastructure; constitutional separation-of-powers and appointment issues must be considered (e.g., Intercollegiate Broadcasting decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow online initial filing with prima facie review
rubrics_metrics.description: A centralized website linked to the Copyright Office site would allow copyright owners to provide proof of registration for their work and to present a prima facie case of infringement; plaintiff’s evidence could be reviewed online by Copyright Office support staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online filing improves access and efficiency; staff would ensure proper service and, if prima facie met, require defendant participation in the administrative proceeding rather than immediate removal to district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require defendant participation in administrative proceeding (no immediate removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff presents a prima facie case of infringement, the defendant would be required to participate in the administrative proceeding online, instead of being allowed to remove the case immediately to district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting immediate removal encourages resolution in the low-cost forum; must preserve appeals to district court (de novo) for fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cap damage awards to keep claims 'small' and incentivize participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement claims brought before the CIRP could remain 'small claims' by capping damage awards at some number that incentivizes participation; that amount could be fixed (perhaps fewer than $30,000) or indexed annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cap balances access and administrative scope; some stakeholders favor retaining statutory damages, costs, and attorney’s fees—policy choice affects who will use CIRP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute damages using licensing estimates, actual profits, or unjust enrichment
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations of damages could be determined based on the proven value of the work, educated estimates of industry licensing fees, demonstration of actual profits lost, or unjust enrichment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgia–Pacific patent factors translate to copyright (e.g., prior royalties, rates for similar work, portion of infringer’s profit attributable to the work); CIRP may assess costs of the proceeding to the infringer as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep process simple to reduce need for counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the CIRP process remains simple, there may be little need to hire an attorney to pursue a claim; costs should be minimal if discovery is limited and proceedings occur primarily online or regionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity increases access for individual creators; but complex defenses (e.g., fair use) may still require counsel or referral to district court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-judge initial ruling within sixty days
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial ruling would be made by a single CIRP judge within sixty days of the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expedited timeline promotes efficiency and quick resolution; plaintiff and defendant submit written records and any affirmative defenses within set timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal without prejudice if affirmative defenses persuasive (re-file option)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of any affirmative defenses that the CIRP judge finds persuasive would result in the complaint being dismissed without prejudice for the plaintiff to re-file in federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserves defendants’ rights to stronger forum for complex defenses while preventing CIRP from being the exclusive route; balances speed with access to full remedies in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo appeal to federal district court
rubrics_metrics.description: If the CIRP judge finds the defendant infringed, the defendant would be able to appeal to any federal district court; consistent with CRJ rulings, an appeal would face a de novo standard of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De novo review provides robust check on administrative findings and addresses constitutional and due-process concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative remedies limited to monetary awards and procedural sanctions (no injunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although as an administrative body it could not issue injunctions, the CIRP would be able to set monetary damages and assess the cost of the administrative proceeding to the infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of injunctive power is a central limitation; plaintiffs needing removal of material from marketplace must still go to federal court; emphasizing monetary damages may align with Supreme Court preferences and licensing-based solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider novel administrative remedies (e.g., enforce Creative Commons attribution, ISP letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CIRP could consider enforcing a Creative Commons attribution license for attribution, interpret attribution under a reasonableness standard, rule on waiver by contract, and issue letters to ISPs about 'repeat offenders'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel remedies could expand non-monetary relief tailored to online harms and social norms; ISP letters could create pressure via contributory liability concerns to limit infringers, but statutory authority and constitutional limits must be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize need for statutory amendment and appointment/constitutional concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a new administrative process and giving CIRP judges certain powers would require Congress to amend the Copyright Act; constitutional separation of powers questions about housing a tribunal of ALJs in the Copyright Office are a large concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must consider Appointments Clause and other constitutional constraints (e.g., Intercollegiate Broadcasting and SoundExchange cases), and legislative willingness depends on political pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize efficiency, access, and deterrence as policy goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A system that provides better access to remedies for copyright infringement could increase the perceived legitimacy of copyright, deter infringement, and alleviate burdens on federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficient monetary remedies could promote licensing, expand lawful use of works, and re-align remedies with normative expectations; however, beware of creating perverse incentives (compulsory-license concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate unresolved problems: lack of injunctions and complexity of fair use
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of injunctive relief and the fact-specific, complicated nature of fair use defenses could be stumbling blocks for the CIRP model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair use touches on free expression, privacy, and competition—issues that may not be fully heard in shortened proceedings; but CIRP judges’ expertise and availability of de novo appeals mitigate some concerns. Remember eBay four-factor injunction test and courts’ hesitance to grant injunctions.
